description:
We’re a team of two who share an interest in space exploration and game development. We’re creating Beyond the Universe, an educational 3D game inspired by real space missions.

We want players to learn how rockets reach orbit, why fuel matters at every stage of a flight, and what makes a landing site safe. By planning a launch, choosing where to land, and collecting samples, players will see how decisions made before liftoff shape what a crew can do on the surface.
summary:
Beyond the Universe is an educational 3D space exploration game developed by Team Deadlock for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Across 18 missions, players plan and fly missions, deploy satellites, dock with the International Space Station, and explore destinations including the Moon, Mars, and an asteroid. Players choose launch vehicles, spacecraft, fuel, and scientific equipment, then discover how these decisions affect their mission. NASA resources and NASA-provided 3D models connect the experience to real spacecraft and exploration objectives. Our goal is to make space mission design understandable through experimentation: players can test a plan, observe the outcome, and improve their approach. The project encourages curiosity about science and engineering while showing how individual decisions shape an entire mission.

To download and play Beyond the Universe on Windows, follow the link at the bottom of the Project Details section.
details:
Beyond the Universe

Beyond the Universe is a 3D educational game for Windows developed by Team Deadlock for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Across 18 missions, players turn a scientific or operational objective into a flight plan. Before launch, they select a launch vehicle, choose a spacecraft and instruments, and compare fuel plans. During flight, they manage thrust, separate stages, and carry out tasks such as deploying a satellite, docking with the International Space Station, or exploring the Moon and Mars.

What can players do during a mission?

The game connects planning decisions to what players see and do in flight. Players can track a satellite after deployment, watch the James Webb Space Telescope unfold, and scan asteroid Bennu to compare potential sampling sites.

How do we use NASA resources in the game?

We integrated publicly available 3D models from NASA’s official website, including MarCO, Webb, OSIRIS-REx, Bennu, and Perseverance. NASA is credited as the source of those models. We also used NASA mission design resources to inform the planning tools and included a reference visualization of an Earth–Moon trajectory.

We built the game with:

  1. JavaScript
  2. HTML
  3. CSS, used Three.js
  4. WebGL for 3D rendering
  5. packaged it for Windows with Electron.

We also used SI:

  1. Google Gemini
  2. Claude
  3. ChatGPT

SI assistants to explore ideas, discuss implementation options, and work through technical questions during development.

How does the game support players with different levels of experience?

We designed the game for players with different levels of experience. Manual controls let players practice maneuvers, autopilot helps newcomers focus on mission objectives, and a separate demo mode opens all 18 missions without budget limits.

What do we want players to learn from the game?

We simplified flight physics and shortened mission timescales to keep the controls approachable and make it easy to test a revised plan. Our goal is to help players understand why choices about fuel, equipment, and timing matter and give them a reason to explore the real missions that inspired the game.

How to Play on Windows

  1. Download Beyond the Universe (ZIP) ← Click here
  2. Extract all files from the ZIP archive.
  3. Open the extracted folder and double-click Beyond the Universe.exe to launch the game.
